title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed research finds the AI capex boom has not moved the US current account: aggregate investment is flat as a share of GDP (reallocated into AI from other sectors), private and business saving have held up, and the widening deficit since 2019 is almost entirely fiscal, though larger planned tech capex could change that.

insights.claim: AI-related imports reached a high of 23 percent of US imports in 2025, yet the current account deficit is largely unchanged because the current account equals national saving minus domestic investment, so large capital-equipment imports do not widen the deficit unless investment outruns saving.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate AI import surge into a wider trade deficit without checking the savings-investment gap.

insights.claim: The US current account deficit widened from about 2.2% of GDP on average in 2015-19 to about 3.7% since 2023, but the widening came almost entirely from the saving side while investment-to-GDP stayed remarkably steady.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: The deficit story is about saving, not AI capex.

insights.claim: Gross domestic investment averaged 21.3% of GDP in the five pre-pandemic years, 21.5% over 2023 to 2026:Q1, and 21.1% over the past four quarters, so the AI boom is invisible in the aggregate investment rate.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: AI capex is crowding out other investment rather than adding to total investment.
insights.locator: Investment Has Been Reallocated, Not Expanded

insights.claim: AI contribution to nonresidential investment is rising but coincides with fading factory construction following the 2022 industrial policy legislation, soft non-tech structures and equipment investment, and declining residential investment.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: Non-AI investment weakness is masking the AI buildout's macro impact.
insights.locator: Investment Has Been Reallocated, Not Expanded

insights.claim: During the dot-com expansion private saving fell by nearly 3 percentage points of GDP (1995-2000) as households spent equity gains; today private saving averages 20.8% of GDP since 2023 versus 21.3% pre-pandemic, a half-point gap partly due to post-pandemic savings unwinding.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: No wealth-effect-driven consumption binge comparable to 2000 shows up in the saving data so far.

insights.claim: Unlike the dot-com buildout led by young telecom firms with thin cash flow, the AI buildout is concentrated in the most cash-generative firms, so business saving has held at 10.9% of GDP over the past four quarters versus about 10.5% pre-pandemic and a dot-com trough near 8.8%.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: Funding profile of AI capex is much sturdier than the dot-com era, lowering a macro-financial instability argument.
insights.locator: Business Sector Saving Has Not Fallen

insights.claim: Government saving fell from about -2.2% of GDP in 2015-19 to about -4.0% since 2023, whereas during dot-com it rose nearly 5 points to a surplus of roughly 4% of GDP on capital-gains tax receipts.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: Fiscal policy, not AI, is the main external-balance driver; ties to Treasury supply and dollar debates.
insights.locator: Government Saving Has Moved in the Opposite Direction

insights.claim: Of the roughly 2.4 percentage point widening in the saving-investment gap versus 2019:Q4, government dissaving accounts for about 1.75 points, lower private saving about half a point and higher investment essentially nothing.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: Decomposition: about 73% fiscal, 20% private saving, ~0% investment.
insights.locator: Decomposing the Contributions to the Current Account Balance

insights.claim: Announced 2026-27 capex plans of major tech firms are considerably larger than what has been built, and if drags on other investment fade as AI capex accelerates, higher investment and lower business saving would widen the current account deficit.
insights.speaker: Julian di Giovanni
insights.so_what: A later-stage AI capex acceleration is the channel through which the external deficit and foreign financing needs could rise.
insights.locator: Caveat and Why Things Could Change
